## Reflections: What This Breakfast Means to Me

Sharing breakfast with Marcus, I feel grounded. Social science backs this up, but it’s the lived experience that matters most to me. Regularly beginning the day together not only keeps our lives in rhythm—it’s also a subtle act of care, an invitation to pause and check in before we both scatter into our daily routines.

Fiese et al. (2012) remind me that sharing meals can improve the ways we communicate and regulate our emotions, even influencing our long-term dietary habits for the better. Grignon (2001) digs deeper, exploring how rituals—like “breaking bread” in the morning—can restore a sense of normalcy in the constantly shifting tempo of modern life. 

**Yet, as Warde (2016) observes in The Practice of Eating, these rituals are far from universal in their form or meaning. The “small, nourishing ceremony” of breakfast can look dramatically different across cultures and family structures. In some households, breakfast is a communal affair, with extended family gathering daily around a shared table, while in others it’s a solitary or on-the-go experience shaped by work schedules or cultural norms. For example, Warde notes that in Scandinavian countries, breakfast might center on open-faced sandwiches and quiet conversation, while in parts of Asia, savory soups or rice dishes are the morning staple, often eaten quickly or even outside the home.**

**Family structure also plays a role: a single-parent household, a multigenerational family, or a group of roommates might each develop their own breakfast rituals, negotiating time, space, and food preferences. Warde argues that these practices are “social accomplishments”—not just habits, but active expressions of identity, belonging, and adaptation to circumstance (Warde, 2016, p. 67).**

Intentional breakfasts—even unpolished ones—help me feel connected: to Marcus, to our city, to the seasons unfolding in the markets. The act of choosing food with care, preparing it alongside someone, and sharing it at the table shapes our sense of hope and continuity.

Today’s meal was simple, beautiful, and enough. I finished breakfast feeling not just nourished, but re-centered and a little more optimistic about whatever the day would bring.
